content: Bedwetting, also known as nocturnal enuresis, refers to involuntary urination during sleep in individuals who have surpassed the typical age at which bladder control is expected to develop. In most cases, bedwetting is attributed to a developmental delay rather than an emotional or physical disorder. Only a small proportion of cases, approximately 5% to 10%, are linked to specific medical conditions. A family history of bedwetting is often observed in affected individuals. Generally, most girls achieve nighttime dryness by the age of six, while most boys do so by the age of seven. By the age of ten, 95% of children are dry at night. The primary symptom of bedwetting is involuntary urination during sleep, typically occurring at least twice per month. To rule out underlying medical conditions such as infections or diabetes, a urinalysis is performed. Imaging studies, such as X-rays of the kidneys and bladder, are not routinely required unless there is a clinical suspicion of other underlying problems. Treatment options for bedwetting range from behavioral interventions, such as the use of bedwetting alarms, to pharmacological therapies, including hormone replacement. In rare cases, surgical procedures, such as urethral enlargement, may be considered. Since bedwetting is often a developmental issue, treatment strategies primarily focus on preserving or enhancing the individual’s self-esteem. Emotional stress and psychological harm can occur if individuals with bedwetting are subjected to feelings of shame or embarrassment. Therefore, treatment guidelines emphasize the importance of counseling parents to avoid applying pressure, shaming, or punishing the child for a condition that is beyond their control. Primary prevention strategies include ensuring adequate sleep and encouraging regular bathroom use during both daytime and nighttime hours, which may help mitigate some aspects of bedwetting.
